data.title: Middle East Eye: Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan activate Mecca Pact amid war with Houthis
data.author: Sean Mathews
data.summary:
Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan activate Mecca Pact amid war with Houthis
Submitted by
Sean Mathews
on
Mon, 10/05/2026 - 21:17
The public deployment of Pakistani and Turkish troops to Saudi Arabia carries symbolic weight across the region
Pakistani Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Foreign Affairs Ishaq Dar, left, Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman Al Saud, centre, and Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan pose during a Strategic Political and Defence Committee meeting in Riyadh, on 5 October 2026 (Turkish foreign ministry handout/AFP)
Off
Turkey and Pakistan said they will undertake a "rapid deployment" of troops to Saudi Arabia as part of their new mutual defence alliance, the Mecca Pact, in a move that could deepen the Houthis' isolation in the region.
The announcement on Monday came after representatives of the three countries held an emergency meeting in Riyadh where they condemned recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, in particular those targeting the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, without mentioning the Houthis by name.
The trio "reaffirmed their unequivocal rejection of any attack or threat against the Kingdom's security and territorial integrity", they said in a joint statement.
They also agreed "to move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defence commitments and to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the Kingdom".
The meeting came as Yemeni government forces backed by Saudi Arabia launched a large-scale offensive whose mission the government said is to retake all the territory the Houthis conquered in 12 years of war.
It's unclear what immediate tactical impact Pakistan and Turkey's deployment to Saudi Arabia will have on the war.
Pakistan already has tens of thousands of troops in the kingdom. Reuters reported last week that Pakistan sent four plane loads of weapons to the port city of Aden to support the Saudi-backed government.

"In response to the Saudi aggression against our country in the past 24 hours ... the Yemeni armed forces targeted King Khaled Airport in Riyadh," the military spokesperson said in a statement.

"The Saudi skies are open theatre for our operations, except for the holy airspaces of Makkah and Madinah," the Houthi warning said.

data.title: Middle East Eye: CIA report warns of civil conflict and 'collapse' in Israel: Report
data.author: Hossam Desouky
data.summary:
CIA report warns of civil conflict and 'collapse' in Israel: Report
Israel is at risk of internal collapse or civil war because of tensions among Israelis, an August report by CIA experts tasked with providing “alternative analysis” said, according to a report by Drop Site News published on Monday.
The CIA report, titled “Fracture From Within", said that Israel faces a volatile situation ahead of 27 October elections, where Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will be fighting for his political future.
The authors noted that one of the most divisive Israeli political issues is the long-standing exemption from military service that ultra-Orthodox Israelis enjoy.
The row has exposed deep divisions within Netanyahu's right-wing bloc and raised questions about whether he will have the support of two ultra-Orthodox parties: United Torah Judaism (UTJ) and Shas - his most dependable allies since he first became prime minister in 1996.
While hundreds of thousands of reservists have been mobilised for Israel’s genocide in Gaza and wars on Lebanon, Syria and Iran, ultra-Orthodox men have historically been exempt from compulsory military service in order to pursue full-time religious studies in yeshivas.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Hormuz Strait disruptions could lead to global food security crisis, International Chamber of Commerce Chief warns
data.author: Mera Aladam
data.summary:
Hormuz Strait disruptions could lead to global food security crisis, International Chamber of Commerce Chief warns
Disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz could lead to a global food security crisis, the secretary general of the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC) John Denton warned.
According to the Wall Street Journal, Denton indicated that if the vital waterway is not reopened, grain prices could rise by up to 80 percent.
The situation in the strait has also caused a shortage of around 2.7 million tons of fertiliser on the world market, a decrease of nearly 40 percent.
Such obstacles could affect international agricultural production and food supplies, making import-dependent countries especially vulnerable.
The report noted that the ICC is working with the UN and the International Maritime Organization on a mechanism that would transfer temporary management of navigation through the waterway to the UN Secretary General.
However, the ongoing tensions between the US and Iran have hindered its implementation, the report added.

data.summary:
Saudi Aramco chief warns of 'scarily thin’ global oil stockpiles, amid war on Iran
The chief executive of Saudi Aramco warned that the world's oil stockpiles are now "scarily thin".
In his first public speech since the US-Israel war on Iran began, Amin Nasser said the conflict reduced oil supply from the region by "nearly 3bn barrels", with over 1bn barrels of oil released from reserves to cushion the depletion.
Nasser estimated that "less than 6bn barrels of commercial inventories remain today, with the vast majority not practically available".
"The system is already straining," he told the Energy Intelligence Forum conference in London. "And with precious little else the world can turn to, the supply resilience cushion is scarily thin."
